title: Euclidean Domains

:::definition{17.2.1} Euclidean domain
An integral domain $R$ is a Euclidean domain (ED) if there exists a function $N : R \setminus \{0\} \to {\ZZ}_{\geq 0}$ (the Euclidean norm) such that for any $a, b \in R$ with $b \neq 0$, there exist $q, r \in R$ with $$a = bq + r, \qquad \text{where } r = 0 \text{ or } N(r) < N(b).$$
:::

:::example{17.2.1} Euclidean domains
- ${\ZZ}$ with $N(a) = |a|$.
- $k[x]$ (for $k$ a field) with $N(f) = \deg(f)$.
- The Gaussian integers ${\ZZ}[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in {\ZZ}\}$ with $N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2$.
- The Eisenstein integers ${\ZZ}[\omega] = \{a + b\omega : a, b \in {\ZZ}\}$ where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$, with $N(a + b\omega) = a^2 - ab + b^2$.
:::
